extracted.intended_audience: general readers, historians, and citizens interested in Benjamin Franklin's civic recommendations and public service practice
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts of procedural recommendations, contractual terms, and public-policy proposals from Franklin's narrative, including street sanitation, post-office reform, colonial-union design, hiring contracts for waggons/horses, and militia/relief provisions. Useful for understanding historical standards and practical specifications used in mid-18th-century public affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mud collection and drainage carts for street cleaning
rubrics_metrics.description: That the mud, when rak'd up, be not left in heaps to be spread abroad again by the wheels of carriages and trampling of horses, but that the scavengers be provided with bodies of carts, not plac'd high upon wheels, but low upon sliders, with lattice bottoms, which, being cover'd with straw, will retain the mud thrown into them, and permit the water to drain from it, whereby it will become much lighter, water making the greatest part of its weight; these bodies of carts to be plac'd at convenient distances, and the mud brought to them in wheel-barrows; they remaining where plac'd till the mud is drain'd, and then horses brought to draw them away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical design details (low bodies on sliders, lattice bottoms, straw covering) to allow water to drain and reduce weight before removal; place carts at convenient distances and use wheel-barrows to bring mud to them. Note: Franklin later expresses doubts about practicability in narrow streets because of obstruction concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweep dust before shops open
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring the dust to be swept up and carry'd away before the shops are open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a practicable seasonal measure (especially in summer when days are long). Franklin observed many shopkeepers leaving tasks until after sunrise and argues sweeping earlier reduces dust being blown into eyes and shops and cumulatively improves urban life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-office reform and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulate several offices, bringing the officers to account to improve the post office's revenues and operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin reports being appointed comptroller to implement improvements; acknowledges that some improvements require initial expense (leading to temporary debt) but can increase clear revenue substantially if properly executed. Implicit criteria: enforce accountability, implement operational improvements even when initially costly, monitor long-term yield (compare to other posts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan for union of the colonies (government structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: General government to be administered by a president-general, appointed and supported by the crown, and a grand council to be chosen by the representatives of the people of the several colonies, met in their respective assemblies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed as a union sufficient for defense and important general purposes. Franklin notes the plan was unanimously agreed to by commissioners but later rejected by assemblies (too much prerogative) and by England (too democratic). The entry includes that a committee (one member per colony) considered plans and that his was preferred with amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raising funds via Loan Office orders (short-term finance mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use orders on the trustees of the Loan Office, payable in a year and bearing interest (proposed at five percent), to raise funds and purchase provisions when direct taxation or governor assent is unavailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a legal workaround: print and issue orders that bear interest and are accepted as payment; they can circulate like money and attract investors because they pay interest while held. Franklin describes rapid uptake and practical success of the method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms for contracting waggons, teams, and horses (advertisement clauses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific contractual conditions for hiring waggons, teams, and horses for military service, enumerated in an advertisement with numbered terms (1–6) and an empowering note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes explicit items: (1) pay rates per diem — waggon with four horses and driver: fifteen shillings; pack or saddle horse with furniture: two shillings; horse without saddle: eighteen pence; (2) pay commences from joining the forces and reasonable allowance for travel time; (3) valuation of lost waggons/teams/horses by indifferent persons chosen between contractor and owner, with that valuation to be paid in case of loss; (4) seven days' pay advanced at contracting if required, remainder to be paid by General Braddock or paymaster on discharge or as demanded; (5) drivers/horse-keepers not to be called upon to do soldier duties or other employment beyond conducting/taking care of their carriages or horses; (6) any forage (oats, corn) brought in excess of the horses' subsistence to be taken for army use with reasonable price paid. Note empowers the contractor's son to contract in a specified county. The advertisement text is used to solicit voluntary service and to discourage forcible impressment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance payment and bonds for contractor assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners insisted on the contractor's bond for performance; the advertisement also provided for seven days' pay in hand as advance when contracting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin gave his bond to assure owners because they did not fully trust General Braddock; he also advanced additional funds personally when general funds were insufficient. The practice underscores use of contractual security and advance payment to secure reluctant suppliers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of relief parcels for subaltern officers
rubrics_metrics.description: A specified list of provisions (per parcel) intended as presents for subaltern officers: 6 lbs loaf sugar; 6 lbs Muscovado sugar; 1 lb green tea; 1 lb bohea tea; 6 lbs ground coffee; 6 lbs chocolate; 1–2 cwt best white biscuit; 1–2 lb pepper; 1 quart best white wine vinegar; 1 Gloucester cheese; 1 kegg 20 lbs butter; 2 doz. old Madeira wine; 2 gallons Jamaica spirits; 1 bottle flour of mustard; 2 well-cur'd hams; 1–2 dozen dry'd tongues; 6 lbs rice; 6 lbs raisins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parcels were packed and placed on horses as presents, intended to supply necessaries and refreshments for officers on a long march; Franklin notes grateful acknowledgements from regimental colonels. This functions as an explicit standard for relief-package composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish and discipline a voluntary militia (legislative design principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft and pass a bill for establishing and disciplining a voluntary militia, taking care to leave conscientious objectors (Quakers) at their liberty and to address objections through explanatory dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Franklin reports successfully carrying the bill through the Assembly and publishing a dialogue answering objections to encourage association and recruitment. Implicit criteria: legislate while protecting religious conscience; accompany legislation with public persuasion materials to overcome objections.
